lesson.title: Representação de palavras e "Bag of Words" (BoW)
lesson.description: A apresentação do conceito de "Bag of Words" (BoW) é o objetivo principal deste encontro. Assim, espera-se que ao seu termino, as pessoas desenvolvedoras possam compreender como essa técnica de representação é utilizada e sua importância na aplicação de PLN.
related_labels: Modelos probabilísticos para extração de informação

before_phase4_candidates.label: Bag-of-Words Model Definition
before_phase4_candidates.description: The BOW model represents text as fixed-length vectors by counting the frequency of each word in the document. It disregards grammar and word order.
coverage_criteria: Explain what BOW model is and how it represents text.
Identify that BOW outputs a vector of word counts.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Simple Explanation of the Bag-of-Words Model

anchors.locator: A Simple Explanation of the Bag-of-Words Model
The bag-of-words (BOW) model is a representation that turns arbitrary text into fixed-length vectors by counting how many times each word appears.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article explicitly defines BOW as 'representation that turns arbitrary text into fixed-length vectors by counting how many times each word appears'.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a foundational concept; students can be asked to define and give an example.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Vocabulary in Bag-of-Words
before_phase4_candidates.description: The vocabulary is the set of all unique words present in the document corpus. It forms the dimensions of the BOW vectors.
coverage_criteria: Define vocabulary in BOW.
Given a set of documents, identify the vocabulary.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Simple Explanation of the Bag-of-Words Model

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article defines vocabulary as 'the set of all words found in our document set' and shows how it determines vector dimensions.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific component of BOW; checking this ensures understanding of vectorization.

before_phase4_candidates.label: BOW Vectorization Steps
before_phase4_candidates.description: To vectorize text with BOW, first determine the vocabulary (unique words), then count occurrences of each word in each document to form a vector.
coverage_criteria: List the two steps of BOW vectorization.
Apply counting to a simple example.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Simple Explanation of the Bag-of-Words Model

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article walks through 'Step 1: Determine the Vocabulary' and 'Step 2: Count' with an example.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a procedural concept; students can be asked to perform the steps on new text.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Context Loss in Bag-of-Words
before_phase4_candidates.description: BOW model loses word order and contextual information, functioning like a literal bag of words: only word presence/frequency counts, not position.
coverage_criteria: Explain why BOW ignores word order.
Describe the trade-off of using BOW (simplicity vs context loss).
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Simple Explanation of the Bag-of-Words Model

anchors.locator: Notice that we lose contextual information, e.g. where in the document the word appeared, when we use BOW. It's like a literal bag-of-words: it only tells you what words occur in the document, not where they occurred.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article states 'Notice that we lose contextual information... It's like a literal bag-of-words: it only tells you what words occur... not where they occurred.'
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Understanding limitations is key; a single question can confirm this concept.

before_phase4_candidates.label: BOW Implementation with Keras Tokenizer
before_phase4_candidates.description: BOW can be implemented in Python using Keras' Tokenizer class: fit_on_texts to build vocabulary, then texts_to_matrix with mode='count' to get count vectors.
coverage_criteria: Explain how to use Tokenizer for BOW.
Write code to fit tokenizer and get count matrix.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article provides a code example using Keras Tokenizer, demonstrating fit_on_texts and texts_to_matrix with count mode.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a practical implementation detail that can be checked with code-oriented questions.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Applications and Strengths of Bag-of-Words
before_phase4_candidates.description: BOW is used in NLP tasks like Text Classification and profanity detection due to its simplicity and low computational cost, despite losing context.
coverage_criteria: Name two applications of BOW.
Explain why BOW is useful despite its simplicity.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: A Simple Explanation of the Bag-of-Words Model

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article mentions 'often used for Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks like Text Classification' and a blog post for profanity detection, and states its strengths: simplicity, inexpensive to compute.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept ties the technique to real-world use; questions can ask about when BOW is appropriate.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Bag of Words (BoW) Definition
before_phase4_candidates.description: Bag of Words is a method to extract features from text documents by creating a vocabulary of all unique words and representing documents as vectors of word counts, ignoring word order.
coverage_criteria: Student can state that BoW is a text representation technique that uses word frequency vectors.
Student can explain that BoW disregards grammar and word order.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: An introduction to Bag of Words and how to code it in Python for NLP

anchors.locator: An introduction to Bag of Words and how to code it in Python for NLP

extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a core concept that can be assessed with a single definitional question and is foundational for later candidates.

before_phase4_candidates.label: BoW Pipeline Steps
before_phase4_candidates.description: The typical BoW process involves cleaning text, tokenizing (splitting into words), building a vocabulary of unique terms, and generating numeric vectors of word counts for each document.
coverage_criteria: Student can list the main steps: clean, tokenize, build vocabulary, generate vectors.
Student can describe that vocabulary is the set of all unique words from all documents.

extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This breaks down the process into a verifiable sequence of steps, each of which can be checked individually.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Tokenization and Stopword Removal
before_phase4_candidates.description: Tokenization is the process of splitting text into tokens (words). Stopwords (e.g., 'a', 'the') are common words with little significance that are often removed to reduce noise and vocabulary size.
coverage_criteria: Student can define tokenization as breaking text into words/tokens.
Student can explain that stopwords are filtered out because they lack useful information for many NLP tasks.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: An introduction to Bag of Words and how to code it in Python for NLP

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article states: 'Tokenization is the act of breaking up a sequence of strings into pieces...' and defines stopwords: 'words which do not contain enough significance...'
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a well-defined subtask of text preprocessing that can be checked with a short exercise or definition.

before_phase4_candidates.label: BoW Vector Representation and Vocabulary Size
before_phase4_candidates.description: Each document is converted to a fixed-length vector equal to the vocabulary size. Each position corresponds to a word, and the value is the count of that word in the document.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain that a document vector length equals the number of unique words in the vocabulary.
Student can compute a simple BoW vector from given word counts.
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: An introduction to Bag of Words and how to code it in Python for NLP

anchors.locator: The length of the vector will always be equal to vocabulary size.

extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a specific, checkable understanding of how BoW vectors are constructed; suitable for a numeric example question.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Sparse Vectors Problem
before_phase4_candidates.description: When the vocabulary is large, document vectors become mostly zeros (sparse). Sparse vectors require significant memory and computation, posing challenges for machine learning algorithms.
coverage_criteria: Student can define a sparse vector as one with many zero entries.
Student can explain why sparsity is problematic for ML modeling (memory, computational complexity).
before_phase4_candidates.source_name: An introduction to Bag of Words and how to code it in Python for NLP

anchors.locator: This is called a sparse vector. Sparse vectors require more memory and computational resources...

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article warns: 'A big document where the generated vocabulary is huge may result in a vector with lots of 0 values. This is called a sparse vector.' and notes the resource demands.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a single, well-defined disadvantage that can be checked with a short explanation.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Implementing BoW in Python
before_phase4_candidates.description: The BoW algorithm can be implemented in Python by writing functions to clean and tokenize text, build a vocabulary from all sentences, and generate count vectors using a fixed vocabulary.
coverage_criteria: Student can outline the key Python functions: word extraction with regex and stopword removal, vocabulary collection, and vector generation using NumPy.
Student can identify that vector generation iterates over each sentence and increments counts for known vocabulary words.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Using NLTK for Stopwords
before_phase4_candidates.description: Instead of manually listing stopwords, Python's NLTK library provides predefined language-specific stopword lists, such as nltk.corpus.stopwords.words('english').

before_phase4_candidates.label: Limitations of BoW
before_phase4_candidates.description: BoW ignores semantic meaning and word order, making it unable to capture context or phrases. It also produces large sparse vectors for large vocabularies.

Student can explain that large vocabularies lead to high-dimensional sparse vectors.

before_phase4_candidates.description: Vetorização (ou extração de características) é o processo de transformar documentos em representações vetoriais numéricas para que algoritmos de ML possam operar, criando uma matriz onde linhas são instâncias e colunas são características.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Bag of Words (BoW): modelo de saco de palavras
before_phase4_candidates.description: Bag of Words é um modelo simples de representação vetorial que trata o texto como uma coleção não ordenada de palavras, codificando significado e similaridade pelo vocabulário compartilhado; documentos com palavras semelhantes são próximos no espaço semântico.

before_phase4_candidates.source_name: Representação vetorial de textos - bag of words

before_phase4_candidates.label: Etapas do algoritmo Bag of Words
before_phase4_candidates.description: O BoW é implementado em quatro etapas: (1) limpar o texto removendo stopwords e pontuação, (2) extrair tokens conforme a necessidade, (3) construir o vocabulário com tokens únicos, (4) gerar vetores de frequência para cada documento.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Vocabulário e esparsidade em BoW

reconciled_candidates.label: Bag-of-Words Core Definition and Representation
reconciled_candidates.description: The Bag-of-Words (BOW) model represents text as a fixed-length vector of word counts or frequencies from a predefined vocabulary, ignoring grammar and word order. It is a fundamental text representation technique for NLP.
coverage_criteria: Define the Bag-of-Words model and explain how it represents documents as vectors.
Given a short vocabulary, produce a BOW vector for a sentence.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: All candidates define BOW similarly as counting word occurrences while disregarding order and context. Merging into one concept avoids redundant representations of the same foundational idea.

reconciled_candidates.label: N-gram Extension to BoW
reconciled_candidates.description: BoW can capture some word order by using n-grams (e.g., bigrams), where tokens are contiguous sequences of n words, providing a richer representation than unigrams alone.
coverage_criteria: Student can define an n-gram as a contiguous sequence of n words.
Student can explain how bigrams improve representation over unigrams, with a simple example.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate describes a standalone enhancement technique not overlapping with other batch concepts, so it forms its own lesson-local concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: Multi-label Classification Setup with BoW
reconciled_candidates.description: For multi-label text classification using BoW, labels are encoded as binary vectors (each element corresponds to a label, multiple 1s allowed), and the model uses a final sigmoid activation with binary cross-entropy loss, enabling independent binary predictions per label.
coverage_criteria: Student can encode labels for a multi-label problem using a binary vector, contrasting with multi-class one-hot encoding.
Student can explain why sigmoid activation and binary cross-entropy loss are preferred over softmax for multi-label classification.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These candidates cover complementary implementation details for multi-label classification (label preprocessing and model output configuration) and together form a single teachable practical concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: Vocabulary Selection for Bag of Words
reconciled_candidates.description: The BoW vocabulary is a predefined list of words, typically chosen by frequency (e.g., the most common 400 words); words not in the vocabulary are ignored during encoding, which impacts model performance and is a key design decision.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain how a vocabulary is built (e.g., using most frequent words, fixed size) and what happens to out-of-vocabulary words.
Student can discuss trade-offs of vocabulary size on model complexity and generalization.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: This candidate addresses a distinct design choice in BoW, not covered by other candidates in this batch, and stands alone as a lesson-local concept.
